nodes.text: Neural retrieval systems are usually trained and evaluated on one dataset, but many deployments have no training data for their target task, so their zero-shot generalization is unclear.
Retrieval is the first step of question answering, claim verification and duplicate-question detection; building a training corpus is time-consuming and expensive.
Prior benchmarks (MultiReQA, KILT) exist, and lexical retrieval such as BM25 has long dominated with neural models now widely studied.
Prior benchmarks are narrow (one task, one domain, small corpora), so architectures cannot be compared for out-of-distribution generalization.
RQ1: does in-domain performance predict zero-shot performance?
RQ2: which retrieval architectures generalize best zero-shot, and at what latency and index-size cost?
RQ3: how much does annotation selection bias affect the comparison of lexical and non-lexical systems?
Build a heterogeneous benchmark and use it to compare ten systems from five families.
BEIR: 18 English datasets, 9 tasks, nDCG@10, standard data format and open-source software.
Evaluate ten public systems zero-shot on the 18 datasets (in-domain MS MARCO reported separately).
Measure latency and index size on a 1M-document DBPedia sample.
Annotate unjudged top-10 hits (holes) on TREC-COVID for all systems, blind to source system, and re-score.
BM25 in-domain 0.228 vs neural; zero-shot averages relative to BM25 range from - 47.7% (DPR) to + 11% (BM25+CE).
Win counts vs BM25 (16/18, 11/18, 9/18); DeepCT, SPARTA fail; BM25+CE fails on ArguAna and Touche-2020.
Dense-model comparisons, GenQ domain pattern, TAS-B length preference, cosine vs dot-product experiment.
Latency and index sizes: re-ranking and late-interaction slowest and largest; dense fast; ColBERT ~900GB for BioASQ.
Hole@10 and nDCG@10 before/after annotation on TREC-COVID.
In-domain performance did not predict zero-shot performance in this comparison.
No single approach is best everywhere; effectiveness trades off against cost; cross-attention and training loss are hypothesized drivers.
TREC-COVID labels favour lexical systems; the same mechanism is expected but unmeasured elsewhere.
A benchmark and a comparative study that show zero-shot rankings differ from in-domain rankings, quantify the accuracy-cost trade-off, and expose label bias on TREC-COVID.
Single evaluation of public checkpoints without variance; systems differ in several respects.
Label-bias study covers only TREC-COVID.
English only; documents truncated to 512 word pieces; text-only; no task-specific models.
Datasets built with diverse pooling; multilingual, long-document and multi-field tasks.
Retrieval methods should be evaluated on a broad range of datasets; later work argues for effect-size analyses across datasets.
Lexical vs neural retrieval; sparse, dense, late-interaction, re-ranking; nDCG@10; relevance judgments (qrels); pooling.

experiment_chains.experiment: X1 Zero-shot comparison of ten systems on 18 datasets
experiment_chains.hypothesis: Not stated as a formal hypothesis; the implicit expectation is that strong in-domain models also generalize.
experiment_chains.falsifier: Models that beat BM25 in-domain fail to beat it zero-shot.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: Zero-shot evaluation on heterogeneous datasets with a single metric makes results comparable; public checkpoints are used because retraining is often infeasible.
experiment_chains.next: Which architectures generalize best raises the question of what they cost to run.

experiment_chains.experiment: X2 Length preference of dense retrievers and similarity-function control
experiment_chains.hypothesis: Not stated as a formal hypothesis; the authors observe a length difference between TAS-B and ANCE and investigate whether the similarity function can produce it.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: Because TAS-B and ANCE differ in backbone, loss and negative mining, the authors train two models identical except for the similarity function.
experiment_chains.next: Effectiveness must be weighed against latency and index size.

experiment_chains.experiment: X3 Latency and index size on 1M DBPedia documents
experiment_chains.hypothesis: Not stated as a formal hypothesis; the paper reports a performance-cost trade-off.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: A common 1M-document sample with stated hardware makes cost comparable.
experiment_chains.next: Since labels determine the scores, the next question is how reliable they are for non-lexical systems.

experiment_chains.experiment: X4 Hole@10 and manual annotation on TREC-COVID
experiment_chains.hypothesis: Stated as motivation: lexical bias in annotation disfavours non-lexical approaches, so filling unjudged hits should help them more.
experiment_chains.falsifier: (not stated by authors); filling holes would change all systems equally.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: TREC-COVID pooled many systems, so it is the most favourable case for fairness; annotators were blind to the source system to avoid preference bias.
experiment_chains.next: End of chain: motivates diverse pooling for future datasets.
